story.title: China’s military seeks Nvidia’s advanced chips for AI capabilities, commission says - CNBC

facts.text: China 's People's Liberation Army has been "actively soliciting" Nvidia 's most advanced semiconductor chips to develop its artificial intelligence-enabled military capabilities, a congressional commission said in a report released Wednesday.

China is making that move as it faces a quality gap between chips produced by Chinese companies, including Huawei and Cambricon , and the more advanced ones produced by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, such as Advanced Micro Devices , the report noted.
The report's findings could fuel concerns about advanced Nvidia chips having found their way to Chinese users amid escalating investigations from Congress and state and federal regulators.

"Although China has made some progress in achieving its goals, it has not yet closed the hardest chokepoints — including the most advanced capabilities in logic fabrication, memory, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, as well as the Nvidia Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) software moat — and likely will not for some time," the report said.

The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission was created by Congress in 2000 with a mandate to monitor and report to Congress the national security implications of the trade and economic relationship between the U.S. and China.
“China is seeking to evade U.S. export controls to gain the most advanced semiconductors that underpin its intelligentization drive,” the commission said.
Separately, Nvidia’s interim chief executive Colette Kress said on Tuesday that the company is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data centre chips to China, Bloomberg reported .
Nvidia sold $2.4bn of them there in the third quarter.
A congressional report says China still trails the US in computing power, largely because of export controls on advanced chips.
The report says chips from Chinese firms such as Huawei and Cambricon still lag those from Nvidia and AMD.
Congress set up the commission in 2000 to report on the security risks of US trade with China.
This week, the Commerce Department issued rules to close that loophole .
The report lands as Nvidia deals with the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation.
Huang quit after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy.
He is due to appear before House panels on 1 December, according to CNBC.

This move followed criticism from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and members of Congress, who said that the Department of Commerce was not doing enough to counter the diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls.
Congress created the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission in 2000 to monitor the implications of the two countries’ trade and economic relations for US national security.
The report’s authors noted that Chinese manufacturers, including Huawei and Cambricon, lag behind Nvidia and other US companies, including Advanced Micro Devices, in producing advanced chips.

According to the commission, China has made some progress but has still not eliminated critical constraints in the production of logic chips and memory chips, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and Nvidia’s CUDA software ecosystem.
The document states that China is attempting to circumvent US export controls to obtain advanced semiconductors needed to enhance military technologies.
The commission believes that the gap in available computing power remains significant, primarily because of US export restrictions on advanced chips.

The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said Wednesday the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is “actively soliciting” Nvidia’s most advanced processors for military AI as China seeks to evade U.S. export controls.
China has advanced its semiconductor industry but has not overcome bottlenecks in advanced logic fabrication, memory, chipmaking equipment or Nvidia’s CUDA software.
The commission said China still faces chipmaking bottlenecks as companies access Nvidia processors through data centers in third countries.
